pack.title: Circuit Basics (sample pack)
pack.description: A short sample pack to try StudyPack: Ohm's law, series and parallel, RC circuits and op-amps, with LaTeX formulas.

questions.prompt: A 12 V supply drives 3 mA through a resistor. What is its resistance?
questions.explanation: R = V / I = 12 V / 3 mA = 4 kΩ. Keep the units straight: volts over milliamps gives kilohms.
questions.sayIt: R equals V over I: 12 volts over 3 milliamps is 4 kilohms.

questions.prompt: What power does a 1 kΩ resistor dissipate with 5 V across it?
questions.sayIt: V squared over R: 25 over 1000 is 25 milliwatts.

questions.prompt: Why can a resistor run hot even when its current is small?
questions.correct: Power rises with the square of current or voltage, so a high voltage across a large R still dissipates
distractors: Resistance always falls with temperature, so a small current draws ever more power over time
Small currents flow unevenly through the film, concentrating heat in one narrow spot of the body
Heat depends only on current, so the resistor value has no effect on how warm it gets in use
questions.explanation: P = V²/R = I²R. With hundreds of volts across it, even a small current means real power. Size the rating from V²/R, not from the current alone.
questions.modelAnswer: Because dissipation is I²R or V²/R. A small current through a large resistance with a high voltage across it can still be watts.

questions.prompt: Doubling the voltage across a fixed resistor changes its power by what factor?
What is the total resistance of 2.2 kΩ and 2.2 kΩ in parallel?
questions.explanation: Equal resistors in parallel give half of one: R/2 = 1.1 kΩ.

questions.prompt: In a series circuit, which quantity is the same through every component?
questions.explanation: One path means one current. Voltages divide in proportion to resistance.

questions.prompt: Why does adding a resistor in parallel always lower the total resistance?
questions.correct: It adds another path for current, so the same voltage drives more total current
distractors: It shares the supply voltage, so each branch sees less voltage than before it was added
Parallel resistors cancel part of each other's value through their mutual heating effects
The new branch raises the supply current limit, which the meter then reads as lower R
questions.explanation: Conductances add in parallel: G = G1 + G2. More conductance means less resistance, and the total is always below the smallest branch.

questions.prompt: A divider has $R_1 = 10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ on top and $R_2 = 10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ below, fed from 12 V. What is the output?
questions.sayIt: Vout is Vin times R2 over R1 plus R2.

questions.prompt: A divider has $R_1 = 20\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ on top and $R_2 = 10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ below, fed from 9 V. What is the output?
questions.sayIt: Vout is Vin times R2 over R1 plus R2.

questions.prompt: A divider has $R_1 = 30\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ on top and $R_2 = 10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ below, fed from 8 V. What is the output?
questions.sayIt: Vout is Vin times R2 over R1 plus R2.

questions.prompt: A divider has $R_1 = 10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ on top and $R_2 = 40\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ below, fed from 5 V. What is the output?
questions.sayIt: Vout is Vin times R2 over R1 plus R2.

questions.prompt: What is the time constant of 10 kΩ with 100 µF?
questions.sayIt: Tau is R times C: 10 kilohms times 100 microfarads is one second.

questions.prompt: After one time constant, a charging capacitor has reached what fraction of the supply?
questions.explanation: $$V(t) = V_s\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)$$ At $t = \tau$ that is $1 - e^{-1} \approx 0.632$. After $5\tau$ it is above 99 %.

questions.prompt: What is the −3 dB corner of an RC low-pass with $R = 1.6\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ and $C = 100\,\mathrm{nF}$?
What is the phase shift of a first-order RC low-pass at its corner frequency?
questions.explanation: At $f = f_c$ the real and imaginary parts are equal, so $\phi = -\arctan(1) = -45^\circ$. It heads to $-90^\circ$ well above the corner.

questions.prompt: What is the gain of a non-inverting amplifier with $R_f = 47\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ and $R_g = 4.7\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$?
Why does an ideal op-amp with negative feedback hold its two inputs at the same voltage?
questions.correct: Its huge open-loop gain drives the output until the input difference is almost zero
distractors: The inputs are joined inside the chip by a low-value resistor that equalises them
Feedback adds the output to both inputs equally, which cancels any difference between them
The supply rails clamp both inputs to mid-rail whenever the output is not saturated
questions.explanation: With gain of 10⁵ or more, any input difference gives a large output change that feedback uses to cancel the difference. This 'virtual short' only holds while the output is not saturated.
questions.modelAnswer: Negative feedback plus very high open-loop gain: the output moves until V+ − V− is tiny, so we treat the inputs as equal.

questions.prompt: An op-amp has a gain-bandwidth product of 1 MHz. What bandwidth is left at a closed-loop gain of 100?
What does common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR) measure?
questions.correct: How well an amplifier ignores signals that appear equally on both inputs
distractors: How much the output can swing before it clips against either supply rail
How quickly the output can change voltage in response to a large input step
How much the gain drifts as the chip warms up during normal operation
questions.explanation: CMRR = Ad / Ac, usually in dB. It matters most where interference such as mains pickup reaches both inputs alike.
